extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalists, and researchers building models or theories of news selection/homepage placement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and empirical criteria for how stories are selected and placed on newspaper front pages (esp. US national news), with emphasis on information channels and source types that predict coverage. Useful for researchers, newsroom analysts, or homepage-prediction modelers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine Channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel category comprising stories that originate from routine, organized source activity (constituted ~58% of front-page stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes official proceedings (legislative sessions, court hearings, agency meetings), press releases from government agencies/corporations/NGOs, press conferences and briefings organized by sources, and non-spontaneous staged events (speeches, ceremonies, ribbon cuttings). These are pre-scheduled, source-attributed, and lower-risk for publishers — hence easier to publish and more likely to appear on the front page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal Channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel category for stories coming through less formal, off-the-record, or indirect flows (~16% of front-page stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes background briefings (off-the-record), leaks from insiders, non-governmental proceedings (think-tanks, conferences), and items drawn from other news organizations' reports. These can produce publishable stories but typically lack the systematic advantages of routine/official channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enterprise Channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel category for reporter-initiated or original reporting (~26% of front-page stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes reporter interviews initiated by reporters, spontaneous events witnessed by reporters, reporter analysis based on independent reporting, and investigations/research by reporters. Enterprise stories are more resource-intensive and less frequent than routine-channel stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official-source prevalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical finding that roughly 78% of US national news sources were US officials (with ~46% federal, ~5% state/local, ~14% foreign), leaving ~22% from non-government sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant bias toward official sources should be considered when evaluating coverage balance or building predictive models — official sources overwhelmingly supply the raw inputs for front-page stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine-Channel Premium
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational implication: stories arriving through official/routine channels have a systemic advantage in newsworthiness and placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because routine-channel items are pre-scheduled, clearly source-attributed, and risk-mitigated, they are more likely to be selected and placed earlier on homepages/front pages. Models or editorial heuristics should weight channel-origin as a major predictor of publishability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press Release Conversion Rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational implication: stories pegged to press releases or briefings are easier to publish; the existence of a release/briefing increases a story's convertibility into print/online coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat presence of a press release or formal briefing as a feature that increases the likelihood and speed of coverage. Editors often use press releases as practical news leads or story pegs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official-Source Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational implication: stories with named federal-official sources outrank stories without — official quotes confer publishability and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named official quotations function as a credibility/authority shortcut in editorial selection. Counting named official sources or the presence of official attribution can improve predictions of placement and survivability through editorial filters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat Anchoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational implication: reporters' beats determine which routine channels they monitor, so coverage mirrors newsroom beat structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beat assignments channel reporters toward particular official routines and institutional sources. When modeling or auditing coverage, account for beat-driven gatekeeping (which routine events are likely to be noticed and picked up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enterprise Cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational implication: investigative/enterprise stories require more reporter time and editorial resources, lowering their production rate and making them structurally disadvantaged relative to routine channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of higher time and resource costs, enterprise stories appear less frequently; resource constraints should be treated as a negative factor for likelihood of front-page placement unless offset by high perceived significance or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel as a master news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Implication for newsworthiness: the information channel (routine vs. enterprise) acts as a primary predictor of whether and how a story is covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Channel-origin should be treated as a central news-value in editorial decision frameworks and predictive models — it often outweighs other story attributes in determining coverage and placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press-release reverse-engineering (feature for prediction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical implication: homepage-prediction models can use whether a story has a corresponding press release as a predictive feature; routine-channel stories should receive more reliable/earlier coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detecting press releases or official announcements related to a story can materially improve automated predictions of headline/front-page timing and placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official-quote density
rubrics_metrics.description: Implication for newsworthiness: stories with multiple federal-official quotations should achieve higher placement and are more likely to survive editorial objectivity rituals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measures of count/density of official quotes (especially federal officials) as a predictor of prominence; high official-quote density correlates with editorial preference and placement advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite-driven agenda reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical implication: high official-source dependence (~80%) means news selection systematically reproduces the agendas of elites with PR capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating media agendas or designing interventions, recognize that reliance on official channels structurally biases coverage toward elite priorities; models of news selection should incorporate measures of source institutional power and PR activity.
